tier_reason: The tech report checked into the repo (doc/UM-CS-2015-018.pdf), published as an ICSE 2016 paper, runs SPEC CPU2006 against AddressSanitizer: 4% average overhead with all detectors versus over 30% for ASan, and DoubleTake beats ASan on 17 of 19 benchmarks. Valgrind's roughly 17x geomean is reported as context. That makes it B; it is not A because SPEC is not public and the CPU is described only as a 2.33GHz 4-core Xeon, with no model number.

corrections.claimed_speedup: On SPEC CPU2006 (ref inputs), 4% average runtime overhead with all three detectors (overflow, leak, use-after-free) and about 3% with overflow detection alone, versus an AddressSanitizer average over 30%. DoubleTake is faster than ASan on 17 of 19 benchmarks. Valgrind Memcheck averages about 17x (geomean, range 4.5x-42.8x) on the same suite. The README states 2% average for overflow detection only.
corrections.hardware: Dual-processor Intel Core 2-era Xeon system, 4 cores per processor at 2.33GHz, 4MB shared L2, 16GB RAM, Linux 3.13, glibc 2.19 (no exact model number)
corrections.caveats: Numbers come from the tech report in the repo's doc/ directory (published at ICSE 2016; the arXiv 1601.07962 and camera-ready copies are blocked here, so small differences from the final paper are possible). The README's 2% figure differs from the report's 3% for overflow-only. Rollback/replay cost is excluded from the overhead measurement. Measured with 2013-era LLVM 3.2 ASan on old Xeon hardware; the code has been unmaintained since 2016. SPEC CPU2006 is not public.

notes: Upgraded C to B: the peer-reviewed paper's tech report is in the repo and compares directly against ASan, with Valgrind as context. The README itself does not mention either baseline. The ICSE venue comes from a WebSearch result; the umass.edu PDF host was blocked (403).
